pos: n. (John Overall, 1559–1619, Regius Professor at Cambridge and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; English Overall, a Lincolnshire family name.
biblical_def: John Overall was Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge, Dean of St Paul's, and at the end of his life bishop of Norwich, and he sat in the First Westminster Company of the Authorized Version, the group that rendered Genesis through the second book of Kings under Lancelot Andrewes. He was a formidable Latinist who was said to have lost the habit of speaking English fluently, and a controversialist in the Cambridge disputes over perseverance, where he held positions the dictionary does not follow. He belongs here for the work that outlasted the controversies. The Westminster company gave English the cadence of the Pentateuch and the historical books, and the plain fact about that company is that it contained men who disagreed with each other and still produced one voice (Rom 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oracle as the communications of God, and version as a translation.
webster_full: OR'ACLE, n. The communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets; the sanctuary or most holy place.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
COMPAN'Y, n. An assemblage of persons; a number of persons united for the performance of something in common.
PRO'FESSOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; an officer in a university.

corruption_summary: A Westminster translator whose company disagreed about much and produced one voice.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern assumption that a committee cannot produce great prose, and its corollary, that the Authorized Version must have had a single secret author. Six companies of some fifty men produced it, working to agreed rules, reading drafts aloud, and submitting everything to a final revision. The method is the opposite of the romantic one and the result is the most durable English book there is.

The principle to recover is that God committed his words to a people and uses many hands to keep them. “Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2). What is committed is itself right and true: “For the word of the LORD is right; and all his works are done in truth” (Psa 33:4). And Luke describes the care such work takes: “to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus” (Luk 1:3).

pos: n. (John Layfield, d. 1617, Fellow of Trinity College and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Layfield, from a northern place-name.
biblical_def: John Layfield was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, a Greek lecturer there, and rector of St Clement Danes in London, and he sat in the First Westminster Company for the Authorized Version. Before that he had sailed with the earl of Cumberland on the expedition to Puerto Rico and written an account of it, which makes him the only translator who had seen a tropical island, and tradition says the company leaned on him for the architectural passages, the tabernacle and the temple, because he had an eye for building. Whether or not the tradition is exact, it names a real requirement: Exodus and Kings are full of measurements, and a translator who cannot picture a structure will produce a page that nobody can picture either. Scripture itself gives the furniture in inventory form and expects it to be understood (2Ki 4:10).

webster_full: TAB'ERNACLE, n. A tent; a temporary habitation; the sacred tent of the Israelites, in which the ark was kept.
CU'BIT, n. In mechanics, the forearm; a measure of length, being the distance from the elbow to the extremity of the middle finger.
AR'CHITECTURE, n. The art of building; particularly, the art of constructing houses, bridges and other buildings.
VOY'AGE, n. A passing by sea or water from one place, port or country to another.

corruption_summary: The translator who had seen a tropical island, and an eye for the tabernacle's measurements.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the impatience modern readers bring to the measured chapters of Exodus, Kings and Ezekiel, which get skipped as inventory. They are inventory, and they are given because the thing described was real and was built to a pattern God specified. A translator who fudges a cubit has fudged the point.

The principle to recover is that intelligibility is the aim of every rendering, and that concrete detail is part of what must come through. “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9). The standard the Levites set is still the standard: “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). And wisdom's own promise is plainness: “the opening of my lips shall be right things” (Pro 8:6).

pos: n. (William Bedwell, 1563–1632, English Arabist and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector, through William; English Bedwell, from a place-name.
biblical_def: William Bedwell was the first Englishman to master Arabic, and he spent his life on it: a lexicon he never finished, an edition of the Arabic epistles of John, grammars, and the training of the next generation of orientalists. He was vicar of Tottenham, then a village north of London, and he sat in the First Westminster Company for the Authorized Version, where his Semitic learning bore directly on the Hebrew. Nobody in England had asked him to learn Arabic and nothing in his parish required it. He did it because the languages of the Near East throw light on the language of the Old Testament, and because a man who loves the text follows it wherever its vocabulary leads. The ready scribe is the Authorized Version's own word for such a man (Ezr 7:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines orientalist as one versed in the eastern languages, and lexicon as a dictionary.
webster_full: O'RIENTALIST, n. An inhabitant of some eastern part of the world; one versed in the eastern languages and literature.
LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary or book containing an alphabetical arrangement of the words in a language, with the definition of each.
SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; one who is skilled in the law; among the Jews, a doctor of the law.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness.

corruption_summary: The first Englishman to master Arabic, vicar of a village that had no use for it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the utilitarian question put to all such learning: what was it for? Bedwell's Arabic served the Hebrew, the Hebrew served the translation, and the translation served three centuries of English-speaking Christians who never heard his name. The chain is long and every link in it is invisible from the next.

The principle to recover is that God gives skill in learning as a gift and that preparation precedes usefulness by years. “he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the LORD God of Israel had given” (Ezr 7:6). The order of a scholar's making is stated twice over: “Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel” (Ezr 7:10). And the gift is named as a gift: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17).

pos: n. (Richard Thomson, d. 1613, Greek and Latin scholar and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Richard, strong ruler; English Thomson, son of Thomas.
biblical_def: Richard Thomson was born in the Netherlands of English parents, which earned him the nickname Dutch Thomson, and he was reckoned by his contemporaries one of the best Greek and Latin scholars in Europe. He edited Latin texts, corresponded with the continental humanists, and sat in the First Westminster Company for the Authorized Version. He was also, by the testimony of men who knew him, sympathetic to the Arminian side in the disputes then dividing the Dutch churches, and his personal habits were the subject of unfriendly comment. The dictionary states both and draws the conclusion it always draws: God used an assembly of men of mixed convictions and mixed character to give the English-speaking world its Bible, and the text they produced is not thereby compromised (Pro 16:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scholar as a man of letters, and providence as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
webster_full: SCHOL'AR, n. One who learns of a teacher; a man of letters; one who has learning, or is eminent for learning.
PROV'IDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
IN'STRUMENT, n. One who or that which is subservient to the execution of a plan or purpose.

corruption_summary: A translator of mixed convictions and mixed report, used for a work that outlasted both.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern instinct to discredit a work by auditing the characters of the men who made it, a method that would dispose of most of the canon of Scripture itself, since it was written by a murderer, an adulterer, a persecutor and a man who denied his Lord three times in one night.

The principle to recover is that God governs instruments he has not first perfected, and that the answer of the tongue is his. “The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD” (Pro 16:1). The man proposes and the LORD directs: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). And the final clause belongs to him: “none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?” (Dan 4:35).

pos: n. (Geoffrey King, fl. 1605–1630, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Cambridge and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Godfrid, God's peace, through Geoffrey; English King, an occupational or nickname surname.
biblical_def: Geoffrey King succeeded Robert Spalding as Regius Professor of Hebrew at Cambridge and sat in the First Westminster Company for the Authorized Version. Almost nothing else is known of him: a fellowship, a chair, a seat in a company of translators, and no surviving book. He is in the dictionary on purpose, as the limiting case of the whole enterprise. Of the roughly fifty men who made the Authorized Version, several are little more than names in a list, and the English Bible is not less theirs for that. The work was corporate and the credit is corporate, which is the Scripture's own way of describing how its words have been carried: a great company of those that published it (Psa 68:11).

HE'BREW, n. The language of the Hebrews; one of the Semitic languages.

corruption_summary: A chair, a seat in a company, and no surviving book.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern demand that a contribution be traceable to an individual before it counts. The Authorized Version carries no byline. Six companies, agreed rules, a final revising committee and a dedication to the king are all it declares about its own making, and that was deliberate.

The principle to recover is that the publishing of the word is a corporate labour and the accounting is by faithfulness, not by attribution. “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). The standard for each member of such a company is one word long: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

pos: n. (Thomas Holland, 1539–1612, Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Aramaic Teoma, a twin, through Thomas; English Holland, from the Lincolnshire district or the Low Countries.
biblical_def: Thomas Holland was Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford and rector of Exeter College, and he worked in the First Oxford Company of the Authorized Version, which rendered Isaiah through Malachi. His contemporaries described him as a man who had the Fathers at his fingertips and a rooted hatred of the Roman errors, and they recorded his habit, whenever he left the college on a journey, of commending the fellows to the love of God and to the hatred of popery and superstition. He died in 1612, a year after the version appeared. The prophets were his portion of it, which is the hardest Hebrew in the canon and the part that most directly testifies of Christ (Joh 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines divinity as the science of divine things, theology, and prophet as one who foretells future events.
webster_full: DIVIN'ITY, n. The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God and his relations to man; theology.
PROPH'ET, n. One that foretells future events; a predicter; a foreteller.
SUPERSTI'TION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples.
REC'TOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities; also, a clergyman who has the charge of a parish.

corruption_summary: Isaiah through Malachi fell to his company, and he died a year after it appeared.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the embarrassment modern readers feel at Holland's parting formula, which sounds harsh until the content is examined. He was not commending hatred of persons. He was commending hatred of a system that had burned his countrymen alive within living memory for owning an English Bible, and he was about to spend his last years giving England the prophets in its own tongue.

The principle to recover is that the prophets testify of Christ and are read rightly only so. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39). On the Emmaus road the Lord did the same with the same books: “he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). And the word outlasts every translator of it: “the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

pos: n. (Richard Kilby, 1561–1620, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Oxford and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Richard, strong ruler; English Kilby, from a Leicestershire place-name.
biblical_def: Richard Kilby was rector of Lincoln College, Oxford, Regius Professor of Hebrew, and a member of the First Oxford Company for the Authorized Version. Izaak Walton tells a story about him that is the best thing written about any translator. Kilby and a friend heard a young preacher spend most of a sermon proving that a certain word in the new version was badly rendered and offering three better alternatives. Afterwards Kilby took the young man aside and told him that the company had considered those three, and ten more besides, and had rejected them all for reasons the preacher had not thought of. The anecdote is about humility before unseen labour, and the dictionary keeps it for that use (Pro 15:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines render as to translate, and rashness as too much haste in resolving or undertaking a measure.
webster_full: REN'DER, v.t. To translate, as from one language into another; to interpret.
RASH'NESS, n. Too much haste in resolving or undertaking a measure; precipitation; inconsiderate readiness or promptness to decide or act.
HE'BREW, n. The language of the Hebrews; one of the Semitic languages.
CRIT'IC, n. A person skilled in judging of the merit of literary works; one who judges with knowledge and nicety.

corruption_summary: He had considered the young preacher's three better words, and ten more, and rejected them all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the confident public correction of a translation by a man who has not done the work, which the internet has multiplied beyond anything Kilby's young preacher could have managed. The remedy is not deference to authority but the honest question: has anyone already weighed this, and what did they decide, and why?

The principle to recover is that an answer given in its season is a good thing and that a judgment given before the hearing is a shame. “A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it” (Pro 15:23). Solomon states the opposite case bluntly: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13). And the teachable man is the one who gains: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).

pos: n. (Richard Brett, 1567–1637, Oriental scholar of Lincoln College and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Richard, strong ruler; English Brett, a Breton, a man of Brittany.
biblical_def: Richard Brett was a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, rector of Quainton in Buckinghamshire for forty years, and a member of the First Oxford Company for the Authorized Version. His monument in his parish church says he was skilled in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldee, Arabic and Ethiopic, and the claim is borne out by the works he published on the Chaldee and Syriac. He is one of several translators who held a country living while carrying a scholar's library in his head, which was the normal shape of English learning before the universities professionalized it. The Old Testament he helped render into English contains the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra, and somebody at the table had to know it (Dan 1:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Chaldee as the language of the Chaldeans, and philology as the study of language.
webster_full: CHAL'DEE, n. The language or dialect of the Chaldeans; the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words, or a desire to know the origin and construction of language.
LIV'ING, n. The benefice of a clergyman; estate appropriated to the support of a minister.
ETHIO'PIC, a. Pertaining to Ethiopia; the ancient liturgical language of the Ethiopian church.

I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.

corruption_summary: Six languages on a country rector's monument, and forty years in one Buckinghamshire parish.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the scholar from the pastor, which produces a divinity faculty with no congregation and a pulpit with no learning. Brett spent four decades in a village and read six languages, and the Authorized Version is partly the product of men in exactly that position.

The principle to recover is that learning is a gift of God, given for use, and that it is compatible with an obscure station. “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17). The scribe is named for his readiness in the law, not his office: “he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses” (Ezr 7:6). And Paul names his own training without apology: “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers” (Act 22:3).

pos: n. (Thomas Ravis, c. 1560–1609, bishop of London and director of the Second Oxford Company)
etymology: Aramaic Teoma, a twin, through Thomas; English Ravis, a family name of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Thomas Ravis was dean of Christ Church, vice-chancellor of Oxford, bishop of Gloucester and then of London, and he directed the Second Oxford Company for the Authorized Version, which rendered the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles and the Revelation. That is the portion of the version most English readers know by heart, and the company that produced it included Henry Savile and John Harmar and worked under a bishop who was simultaneously administering a diocese. Ravis was a hard man against Puritan nonconformity in his see, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise. His company gave English the Sermon on the Mount, the parables, the passion narratives and the last chapters of the Revelation, and the sword they put into its hand has cut in directions he would not have chosen (Heb 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gospel as the history of the birth, life, actions, death and resurrection of Christ, and twoedged as having two edges.
webster_full: GOS'PEL, n. The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection, ascension and doctrine of Jesus Christ.
TWO'EDGED, a. Having two edges, or edges on both sides; as a twoedged sword.
DISCERN'ER, n. One who discerns, distinguishes, discovers or judges.
DI'OCESE, n. The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom.
scriptures: Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
corruption_summary: His company gave English the Gospels, the Acts and the Revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a translation serves the party that commissioned it. The Authorized Version was produced under a king who wanted the Geneva notes suppressed and bishops who wanted conformity, and within forty years it was the Bible of the New England separatists, the Baptists and the regicides. A faithful rendering is not a tool, because the text has its own edge.

The principle to recover is that the word is living, active and no respecter of the hand that publishes it. “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12). The Lord's own diagnosis of religious error is ignorance of this text: “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God” (Mat 22:29). And the last book closes its own canon against tampering: “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18).

“Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures” (Mat 22:29) — a bishop hard against nonconformity.
“If any man shall add unto these things” (Rev 22:18) — and the sword cut where he would not have chosen.

pos: n. (Sir Henry Savile, 1549–1622, warden of Merton, provost of Eton, and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Heimerich, ruler of the house, through Henry; English Savile, from a Norman place-name.
biblical_def: Henry Savile was a layman, a mathematician, and the only man in the Second Oxford Company who was not a clergyman. He was warden of Merton College and provost of Eton, taught the Almagest at Oxford, founded the Savilian chairs of geometry and astronomy that still exist, and produced the eight-volume edition of the Greek works of Chrysostom that was the greatest piece of English patristic scholarship of its century and nearly ruined him financially. He sat with the company that rendered the Gospels, the Acts and the Revelation. His presence there says something the dictionary wants said plainly: the Authorized Version was not made by clergymen alone, and the mathematician at the table was there because Greek is Greek (1Co 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mathematics as the science of quantity, and patristic as pertaining to the ancient fathers of the Christian church.
webster_full: MATHEMAT'ICS, n. The science of quantity; the science which treats of magnitude and number.
PATRIS'TIC, a. Pertaining to the ancient fathers of the Christian church.
GEOM'ETRY, n. Originally, the art of measuring the earth; the science which treats of the properties of magnitudes.
LA'ITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy; the body of the people not in orders.
scriptures: Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
corruption_summary: A mathematician and a layman at the table where the Gospels were rendered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in two directions. One treats Bible translation as a clerical monopoly, as though ordination conferred Greek; the other treats it as a purely technical exercise in which belief is irrelevant. Savile refutes both. He was a layman with no cure of souls and world-class Greek, sitting among ministers, and the rules of the enterprise bound them all alike.

The principle to recover is that the words themselves are taught by the Holy Ghost and are to be handled as such, by whoever handles them. “Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth” (1Co 2:13). Learning is God's gift wherever it is found: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17). And the deposit was committed to a people, not to a caste: “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2).
